analysis.one_liner: Keeps recent and fully paid medical bills off people's credit reports.
analysis.headline: The Medical Debt Relief Act of 2015, introduced by a Democrat with 11 cosponsors including 6 Republicans, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that credit bureaus could not put a medical bill on someone's credit report until the bill had been delinquent for at least 180 days, and would require them to remove it entirely once it was paid or settled (45 days after payment). It would also change the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to give people a 180-day window: a debt collector would have to send written notice with the exact date reporting could begin, and could not report the debt during that window — giving the person time to check insurance coverage, apply for financial assistance, or settle the bill before it ever touched their credit. The bill took effect six months after enactment [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: People who get sick and end up with medical bills — the roughly tens of millions of Americans with medical debt on their credit reports. A single hospital stay can produce bills that are disputed, insurance delays, or later forgiven by charity care, yet the mere act of a bill being sent to collections can immediately drag down a credit score. The bill would give people a six-month cushion to work out insurance or financial assistance before the debt hit their report, and would erase the damage entirely once a medical bill was paid or settled [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with medical bills in collections

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits consumer reporting agencies from including any medical debt that was placed for collection less than 180 days before the report, so a fresh medical bill cannot instantly damage a credit score.
Requires credit bureaus to exclude a fully paid or settled medical debt 45 days after payment, so paying off a medical bill actually cleans up the credit report.

Requires debt collectors to send written notice before reporting a medical debt, including the specific date reporting could begin, and bars them from reporting the debt during the 180-day window — time the consumer can use to check insurance coverage or apply for financial assistance.

analysis.who_pays: Debt collection agencies and the credit reporting bureaus, whose business depends on collecting and selling consumer debt data. They would lose the ability to use immediate credit reporting as leverage on fresh medical bills and would have to purge paid medical debts. Lenders would also see somewhat less complete information about borrowers' unpaid medical bills during the 180-day window [S3].

drawbacks.text: The delay is real but partial: after 180 days an unpaid medical debt would still be reported, so the underlying problem of medical debt damaging credit for years afterward remains untouched.

Lenders would have a 180-day blind spot on borrowers' unpaid medical bills, and creditors' common argument is that hiding this risk from underwriting can push up rates or tighten lending for everyone; the bill's own stated purpose of 'more perfect information' in credit markets sits awkwardly with excluding information.
The bill does nothing to lower medical bills themselves or to rein in the aggressive collection practices outside of credit reporting; it only limits what appears on the report.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest, well-targeted fix: it does not forgive debt or restrict collection generally, it just stops a medical bill from wrecking a credit score the moment it goes to collections and erases the damage once it is paid. The cost to lenders is a temporary and narrow information gap, and the burden falls mostly on debt collectors and credit bureaus, who would lose a source of leverage and data. The main honest criticism is that it treats a symptom — six months of protection and cleanup — while leaving medical debt itself and long-term reporting untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee in May 2015, and the committee never took it up — no markup, no vote, nothing — before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. John Carney (D-DE) introduced the Medical Debt Relief Act of 2015 on May 15, 2015, joined by Rep. Andy Barr (R-KY) as an original cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day it was introduced, and that was the last action ever taken on it.
The bill gathered 11 cosponsors — 6 Republicans and 5 Democrats — but never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or a companion Senate action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection agencies and credit reporting bureaus are better off: they kept the ability to report fresh medical debts immediately and to keep paid-off medical debts on credit reports, and no comparable bill became law. Patients with medical bills in collections gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 6 of the 11 cosponsors were Republicans joining a Democratic sponsor — but no vote ever took place, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would bar collectors from reporting a medical debt for 180 days and require written notice first, removing immediate credit reporting as a lever to make people pay quickly. Patients would gain time to resolve the bill through insurance or charity care instead.

Bureaus would have to keep fresh medical debts and paid-off medical debts off credit reports, reducing the data in the reports they sell to lenders. What they lose is exactly the information consumers with medical bills most want removed.

Providers would wait longer to see revenue from patients who sent bills to collections, but many would benefit when patients used the 180-day window to pursue insurance coverage or financial assistance rather than defaulting.
